claims.text: The full complement of solutes in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni promotes enhanced short-range order during deformation.
The full complement of solutes in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni promotes nanoscale solute clustering during deformation.
Chemically ordered nanoscale clusters act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Cluster-mediated dislocation pinning increases strain hardening.
Cluster-mediated dislocation pinning delays plastic instability.
Removing one or more elements from the quinary alloy reduces short-range ordering or nanoscale clustering in its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
The alloys compared are equiatomic, single-phase FCC materials produced by thermomechanical processing with matched grain sizes.
Three-dimensional atom-probe tomography can quantitatively compare short-range order and nanoscale solute-cluster distributions before and after deformation.
The quinary alloy has a higher probability of local chemical ordering than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Local chemical ordering in the quinary alloy produces discrete clusters.
Interactions between the clusters and dislocations produce local strain heterogeneities.
Quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit fewer or less pronounced short-range-order clusters than the quinary alloy.
The quinary alloy will exhibit a higher strain-hardening rate than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The quinary alloy will exhibit later necking or plastic instability than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Differences in thermomechanical processing, grain-boundary effects, residual stress, or minor phase inhomogeneity could confound attribution of the mechanical response to short-range order.
Statistically indistinguishable short-range-order patterns combined with notably different mechanical responses would falsify the proposed explanation.
